edition.locus: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia (archive bub_gb_DY2xvRwPetMC), Latin column, chapter II, printed pp. 43-44 (PDF pages 67-68)

source_text: Corpus nostrum cum movetur, aut extrinsecus, aut intrinsecus movetur. Non moveri illud extrinsecus, ex eo patet: quod neque impulsione, neque tractione movetur, sicut ea quae sunt inanimata. Cum autem moveatur intrinsecus, non tamen naturaliter movetur ut ignis. Nam ignis quandiu est, nunquam motum intermittit: at corpus ubi mortuum fuerit, moveri desinit, licet tamen sit corpus. Quare si neque extrinsecus movetur, sicut inanimata; neque naturaliter, velut ignis: manifestum est moveri ab Anima, quae etiam vitam ipsi subministrat. Si igitur corpori nostro vitam ab anima praeberi constet, anima etiam ex suis effectis cognoscitur.
thought_title: That the soul exists: it moves the body and gives it life
orientation: The body moves neither from outside, like lifeless things, nor by its own nature, like fire, since it stops moving at death; so it is moved by the soul, which gives it life.
pass_a_gloss: Our body, when it is moved (movetur), is moved either from outside (extrinsecus) or from inside (intrinsecus). That it is not moved from outside is evident (patet) from this: that it is moved neither by pushing (impulsione) nor by drawing (tractione), as the things that are inanimate (inanimata). But although it is moved from inside, it is nevertheless not moved naturally (naturaliter), as fire (ignis). For fire, as long as it exists, never interrupts (intermittit) its motion; but the body, when it has died (mortuum fuerit), ceases (desinit) to be moved, although it is nevertheless a body. Therefore if it is moved neither from outside, as inanimate things, nor naturally, like fire, it is manifest (manifestum) that it is moved by the soul, which also supplies (subministrat) life (vitam) to it. If therefore it stands established (constet) that life is furnished (praeberi) to our body by the soul, the soul also is known from its effects (effectis).

choices.term: cum autem moveatur intrinsecus, non tamen
choices.english: though it is moved from within, it is still not
rejected: when it is moved from within, it is not

choices.why: The motion proper to a thing's nature, as fire rises.

pass_b_english: When our body moves, it is moved either from outside or from within. That it is not moved from outside is clear from this: it is moved neither by pushing nor by pulling, as inanimate things are. And though it is moved from within, it is still not moved by nature, as fire is. For fire never stops moving as long as it exists, but the body, once it has died, ceases to move, even though it is still a body. If, then, it is moved neither from outside, like inanimate things, nor by nature, like fire, it is plain that it is moved by the soul, which also supplies it with life. So if it is established that the soul gives our body its life, then the soul is also known from its effects.
notes: 'cum autem moveatur intrinsecus, non tamen' taken as concessive ('though ... still not').
'naturaliter' rendered 'by nature' (the motion proper to a thing's nature, as fire rises).
'inanimata' rendered 'inanimate things' throughout sections 3 and 5 to keep the animate/inanimate pair of section 5 consistent.
